summary: Specifies how to translate the body of a message between X.400 and RFC 822 mail. It complements RFC 1327, which covers translation of the envelope and headers. It was replaced by RFC 2156.

eli5.summary: A letter has an envelope and a page inside. Another memo converts the envelope, and this one converts what is written on the page.

questions: map x.400 message body to rfc 822
x.400 and internet mail gateway body conversion
how to map x.400 to rfc 822
subtitle: How a gateway converts message bodies between X.400 mail and Internet (RFC 822 / MIME) mail.

tldr.problem: X.400 (the OSI Message Handling System) and Internet RFC 822 mail structure message bodies differently, so gateways need agreed rules to convert them without losing content.
tldr.mechanism: Body parts are mapped to MIME content-types through an IANA equivalence table, multipart messages map to multipart/mixed or multipart/digest, and special MHS heading extensions carry the extra MIME semantics so the conversion can be reversed.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 2156, so it is a historical definition of the body mapping.

today: RFC 1495 was obsoleted by RFC 2156, so it is no longer the current definition of this mapping. It updated RFC 1327 and was published in August 1993 as a Proposed Standard.

sections.title: Bridging Two Mail Worlds
sections.content:
Internet mail is defined mainly by RFC 822, where a message has headers and a free-form body. MIME (RFC 1341) adds structure to message bodies. The OSI Message Handling System (MHS), often called X.400, is a separate framework developed in 1984.

The earlier RFC 1327 maps the envelope and headers between the two. This memo complements it by mapping the message body, and it updates RFC 1327. The mappings are largely symmetrical, although the MIME semantics are somewhat richer, so MHS heading extensions carry the additional MIME semantics to keep the conversion reversible.
sections.eli5: One memo already explains how to translate the envelope of a letter. This one explains how to translate the page inside.

sections.title: Approach and the Equivalence Table
sections.content:
The mappings are designed for three scenarios: a MIME user and an MHS user exchanging arbitrary binary content, MIME content-types tunnelling through an MHS relay without loss, and MHS body parts tunnelling through a MIME relay without loss.

To help, the IANA keeps the IANA MHS/MIME Equivalence Table. An enterprise that registers an OID for an MHS body part should also register a matching MIME content-type, which in practice is application with a suitable subtype. A new MIME type without an entry gets an OID from the arc defined in this memo.
sections.eli5: A shared phrasebook lists which word in one language matches which word in the other, so translators do not have to guess.

sections.title: Mapping X.400 to RFC 822
sections.content:
An MHS message has an IPMS.heading and an IPMS.body, which is a sequence of body parts. A single body part becomes the MIME content for that part. A forwarded message (IPMS.MessageBodyPart) is mapped recursively. Other parts are looked up in the Equivalence Table, and unknown ones become application/x400-bp.

Several body parts become multipart/mixed, unless all of them are messages, in which case the result is multipart/digest. Order is preserved. One special case: a body that is a single IA5Text part is not marked as MIME at all, so plain RFC 822 mailers do not invoke MIME functions needlessly.
sections.eli5: If there is one page, copy it over. If there are many pages, staple them in the same order into one bundle.

sections.title: Mapping RFC 822 to X.400
sections.content:
Without a MIME-Version header, the body becomes one IA5Text body part with the default repertoire. With one, the symmetric mapping applies to any atomic body part, multipart/mixed, multipart/digest and message/rfc822. Three cases are asymmetric.

  • message/external-body is mapped into a body part as defined in the companion document, RFC 1494.
  • message/partial is mapped to a message with a partial-message heading extension carrying number, total and id.
  • A nested multipart becomes an IPMS.MessageBodyPart with one body part per contained type. The gateway must generate IPMS.this-IPM and should generate a subject, such as 'Multipart Message' for mixed or 'Message Digest' for digest.

Every multipart type also gets a multipart-message heading extension whose enumerated value is mixed(1), alternative(2), digest(3) or parallel(4). When it is present on the way back, the matching multipart type is generated.
sections.eli5: Going the other way, the translator adds a small sticky note saying what kind of bundle it was, so it can be rebuilt exactly later.

sections.title: Header Text and Character Sets
sections.content:
Section 4 changes some of the header rules from RFC 1327 for human-readable text such as Subject and free-form names. The aim there is to render characters well in the remote character set, not to maximize reversibility.

From X.400 to RFC 822, ASCII text is copied, text in an IANA-registered character set becomes encoded-words as in RFC 1342, and anything else uses the X.408 mappings to IA5. In the other direction, an encoded-word is converted to T.61 if all its characters map, and otherwise copied directly into the T.61 string.
sections.eli5: Names and subject lines with special letters get translated carefully so they still look right to the reader at the other end.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document has no explicit security provisions, but warns about two things it maps between the systems. One is the transfer of binary files. The other is strong content typing, which can be used to automatically launch applications on the contents and leave the user exposed to application-specific viruses, such as a spreadsheet macro or a Postscript command that deletes files.
sections.eli5: Mail can carry programs that run by themselves. Opening them automatically could be risky, like opening a parcel that sets off a trap.
